title: Class Relationships & Coupling
description: Deep comparison of Association, Aggregation, Composition, Inheritance, Dependency, and Realization using the same real-world domain example.

topics.title: Association ('uses a')
topics.description: A structural 'uses a' relationship where two independent objects interact without owning each other's lifetimes.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Association is a structural relationship where one class holds a persistent reference or pointer to another class to use its services without claiming lifecycle ownership.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Objects in a domain model must collaborate (e.g., a Student enrolls in a Course). Neither object owns the other's lifecycle.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Class A knows about Class B. When Class A is destroyed, Class B continues to exist completely unaffected.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: In C++, Association is represented by holding a raw pointer (Course*), a reference (Course&), or a std::shared_ptr<Course>/std::weak_ptr<Course>.

sections.content: Association Diagram:

sections.content: Student-Course Association in C++:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Line 13: std::vector<Course*> stores non-owning pointers. When Student is destroyed, courses remain in memory.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Doctor and Patient, Customer and Product, Driver and Car Rental reservation.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when two peer domain entities need to interact without lifecycle dependencies.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use simple association when one object strictly owns the creation and destruction of the other (use Composition).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Loose coupling; objects can be reused independently.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Potential dangling pointers if an associated object is deleted while other objects hold pointers to it.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Unidirectional Association, Bidirectional Association, Many-to-Many Association.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Deleting associated pointers in the destructor (accidental deletion of shared objects).

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How do you prevent dangling pointers in bidirectional associations in C++?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Use std::weak_ptr instead of raw pointers, or implement an explicit unregister/observer pattern where objects notify each other before destruction.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement a bidirectional Association between Author and Book without creating cyclic ownership memory leaks.

practice.title: Bidirectional Association Practice
practice.problemStatement: Link Author and Book without memory leaks.
practice.hint: Use raw non-owning pointers or std::weak_ptr.

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Association represents peer-to-peer relationships with independent lifecycles.

topics.title: Aggregation ('has a' - weak ownership)
topics.description: Weak container ownership where child objects can belong to multiple parents and outlive the container.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Aggregation is a specialized 'has-a' relationship (whole-part) where the container (whole) references parts that have an independent lifecycle outside the container.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: A Department has Professors. If the Department is closed, the Professors do not cease to exist; they can be transferred to another department.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Whole-part relationship with weak ownership. The child outlives the parent.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Represented in C++ using collections of non-owning raw pointers (std::vector<Professor*>) or std::shared_ptr<Professor>.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Department and Professor Aggregation (Hollow Diamond ──◇):

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Aggregation Implementation in C++:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Lines 21-23: ~Department() does NOT delete professors. profKnuth outlives the department scope.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: University Department and Faculty, Sports Team and Players, Playlist and Songs.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use Aggregation for whole-part systems where components can be shared or outlive the parent container.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use Aggregation when the child is strictly created and destroyed with the parent (use Composition).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Allows flexible resource sharing and transfer between containers.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Requires external lifetime coordination so containers don't hold dangling pointers.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Shared pointer aggregation, Observer list aggregation.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Calling delete on aggregated pointers inside the container's destructor.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the key difference between Composition and Aggregation?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: In Composition, the child's lifetime is bound to the parent (child dies with parent). In Aggregation, the child exists independently and can outlive the parent container.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Model a MusicPlaylist aggregation containing Song* pointers.

practice.title: Music Playlist Aggregation
practice.problemStatement: Implement a playlist that references shared songs.
requirements: Destroying playlist does not delete songs

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Aggregation represents weak whole-part relationships where parts exist independently of the container.

topics.title: Composition ('has a' - strong ownership)
topics.description: Exclusive lifetime ownership where the parent object manages the complete creation and destruction of its child components.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Composition is a strong whole-part relationship where the child component has no independent existence outside the parent. The child is created by the parent and destroyed when the parent dies.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: It encapsulates internal subsystems (e.g., a Building owns Rooms). If the Building is demolished, all Rooms are destroyed simultaneously.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Strict lifetime ownership (Filled Diamond ──◆).

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: In C++, Composition is implemented via direct value members (Engine engine;) or std::unique_ptr<Engine>.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Composition Diagram:

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Production C++ Composition with Automatic Cleanup:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Line 19: std::vector<Room> rooms; holds rooms by value. When Building goes out of scope, vector automatically calls ~Room() for all 3 rooms.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: TCP Packet header + payload, ChessBoard and Squares, Desktop Window and Titlebar.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use Composition whenever child objects are strictly internal parts that cannot exist without the parent.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use Composition when objects need to be shared across multiple containers.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Deterministic automatic destruction; zero risk of memory leaks.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: High coupling between parent and child implementation.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Direct Value Composition, Exclusive Smart Pointer Composition (std::unique_ptr).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Leaking raw pointers to internal composite members that outlive the parent object.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How does C++ implement Composition with polymorphic child types?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Use std::unique_ptr<IChildInterface>. This preserves exclusive lifetime ownership (Composition) while allowing the parent to hold polymorphic derived implementations.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Model a CpuProcessor that has Composition with ALU and Registers.

practice.title: CPU Hardware Composition
practice.problemStatement: Implement CPU composition with ALU and Registers.

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Composition is the strongest form of association, guaranteeing tightly bound lifetime and encapsulation.

topics.title: Inheritance ('is a') vs Realization ('implements')
topics.description: Class extension with concrete code reuse vs Interface implementation contracts in C++.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Inheritance (──▷) inherits both interface and implementation code from a base class. Realization (..▷) implements a pure abstract interface contract without inheriting state.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Distinguishing between code reuse (inheritance) and contract fulfillment (realization) prevents bloated, tightly coupled class hierarchies.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Inheritance = Is-a subclass. Realization = Implements interface behavior.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Inheritance: class Dog : public Animal (inherits fields and methods). Realization: class Button : public IClickable (overrides pure virtual functions).

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Comparison Matrix:

comparison.title: Inheritance vs Realization Matrix
rows: Multiple inheritance can cause diamond problem

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Inheritance vs Realization in C++:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Line 19: User : public Entity, public ISerializable combines inheritance of state with realization of a serialization contract.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Java-style implements Serializable, Cloneable mapped to C++ pure virtual mixins.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use Realization for capabilities (e.g. IComparable, IClonable, IObservable). Use Inheritance for genuine domain subtypes.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use inheritance just to share a utility function (use composition or free functions).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Realization avoids the diamond problem and enables true decoupling.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Realization provides zero default code reuse without helper mixins.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Interface realization, Abstract class partial realization.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Putting state member variables inside an interface class.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Does C++ have an explicit interface or implements keyword like Java/C#?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: No. C++ implements interfaces using abstract classes containing only pure virtual functions (= 0) and virtual destructors, and implements realization using public inheritance.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Design an IComparable interface and realize it in a Product class comparing by price.

practice.title: IComparable Realization
practice.problemStatement: Realize IComparable in a Product class.

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Realization enforces contract compliance without the tight coupling of state inheritance.

topics.title: Dependency ('depends on')
topics.description: The weakest relationship: temporary method parameter, local variable, or return type dependency.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Dependency (..>) is a transient relationship where class A uses class B temporarily (as a method argument, local variable, or return value) without holding a persistent member variable.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Minimizing persistent state relationships keeps classes decoupled and lightweight.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: A change to Class B may require Class A to change, but Class A does not store Class B in memory.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Syntax in C++: void generatePdf(const Invoice& inv);.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Dependency Flow (Dashed line with open arrow ..>):

callout.title: Dependency in C++
callout.text: PrinterService - - - > Invoice: PrinterService receives Invoice as a parameter in print(Invoice i), but does NOT have Invoice as a member variable!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Transient Dependency in C++:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Line 13: InvoicePrinter holds NO instance of Invoice; it depends on it only during the execution of printToPaper().

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Formatters, Serializers, Validators, and Utility math libraries.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use Dependency for stateless helper operations and utility services.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not pass an object as a parameter repeatedly if the caller logically owns it long-term (use Association/Composition).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Lowest possible coupling between classes.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Requires passing parameters at every call site.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Parameter Dependency, Local Variable Dependency, Return Type Dependency.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Unnecessary heavy #include in headers when a forward declaration in header + include in .cpp suffices.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How does Dependency Inversion (DIP) alter classic Dependency relationships?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Classic dependency: High-level class depends on Low-level concrete class (A -> B). With Dependency Inversion: Both High-level and Low-level classes depend on an Abstraction (A -> I <- B), inverting the direction of runtime coupling.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Create a stateless CsvExporter class that depends on a std::vector<User> parameter.

practice.title: Stateless Exporter Dependency
practice.problemStatement: Build a CsvExporter dependent on User collections.
practice.hint: Loop through users and print CSV string.

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Dependency is the most decoupled relationship, representing temporary method-level collaboration.

topics.title: The Master Class Relationship Comparison Matrix
topics.description: Comprehensive comparative matrix mapping all 6 class relationships with lifetime, ownership, coupling, and C++ code representations.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: A unified comparative master guide analyzing all 6 class relationships across 7 critical architectural dimensions.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: LLD interviewers frequently test your ability to explain the subtle trade-offs between Association, Aggregation, and Composition.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Coupling and lifetime ownership form a spectrum: Dependency (weakest) -> Association -> Aggregation -> Composition -> Inheritance (strongest).

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Analyze ownership (Who calls delete?), lifetime (Can child outlive parent?), and C++ memory representation.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Automotive telematics, flight reservation systems, and enterprise banking architectures.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Review this matrix before any Low-Level Design interview to choose relationships consciously.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not default to Inheritance when Association or Composition solves the problem with lower coupling.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Provides a standardized mental checklist for evaluating coupling and lifetime.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: None.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Full spectrum analysis.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Choosing Inheritance when Composition is needed, creating brittle base classes.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Rank the 6 relationships from lowest coupling to highest coupling.

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Dependency (lowest) -> Association -> Aggregation -> Realization -> Composition -> Inheritance (highest coupling).

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Identify the relationship in: Order and OrderItem (Composition), Order and Customer (Association), Order and CreditCardPayment (Dependency).

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Understanding the relationship spectrum is the foundation of elegant, maintainable object-oriented software architecture.
